edges.description: Once in the blood the spirochete must evade innate complement killing to establish infection.
Inoculated spirochetes enter the bloodstream and disseminate as a high-density spirochetemia.
Complement evasion allows survival and expansion of bloodstream Borrelia.
High-density bloodstream expansion creates the antigenic-variation dynamics that drive recurrent bacteremic waves.
The circulating spirochete burden sets the severity of the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction precipitated when antibiotics lyse the organisms.
High-level bacteremia is accompanied by thrombocytopenia, which underlies the petechial rash and bleeding.
Spirochete burden in the liver produces hepatocellular damage and jaundice.
Spirochete burden in the reticuloendothelial system enlarges the liver and spleen.
High-level bacteremia is accompanied by a moderate normochromic anaemia.
Spirochetes in the myocardium produce a perivascular interstitial myocarditis in severe and fatal disease.
Severe disseminated infection can progress to acute respiratory distress syndrome.
Splenic involvement in severe disease can lead to spleen rupture with massive haemorrhage.
Hepatic involvement can progress to hepatic failure in severe cases.
Severe disease can trigger disseminated intravascular coagulation leading to intracranial, gastrointestinal, pulmonary or peripartum haemorrhage.
Central nervous system involvement can present as meningitis, a reported LBRF-specific neurologic complication.
Each new vmp serotype restarts bacteremia, producing the next febrile episode.
Antibody clearance of the dominant serotype selects for spirochetes that have switched to a new vmp, driving the next wave.
The waxing and waning bacteremic waves present clinically as recurrent fever.
Each bacteremic wave drives an abrupt high fever at the onset of the attack.
Headache is among the earliest symptoms accompanying the febrile wave.
Generalized muscle pain accompanies the acute febrile episode.
Joint pain accompanies the acute febrile episode.
Abdominal pain is a common symptom of the acute febrile attack.
The mechanism node manifests clinically as the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction.
The chill phase of the reaction produces acute, intense rigors within hours of the first antibiotic dose.
Cytokine-driven systemic vasodilatation during the flush phase causes a fall in blood pressure and potential collapse.
Thrombocytopenia, rather than vasculitis, produces the petechial rash.
Thrombocytopenia and coagulopathy underlie the bleeding tendency, including epistaxis.
Crowding and poor hygiene increase body-louse infestation, raising the probability of inoculation with B. recurrentis.
Delousing clothing removes the vector, preventing inoculation of B. recurrentis.
Crowded transit and refugee conditions during forced migration promote body-louse infestation and B. recurrentis acquisition.

nodes.description: LBRF is cured by a single dose of a tetracycline (tetracycline or doxycycline), erythromycin, chloramphenicol, or penicillin. Tetracycline clears spirochetes fastest and best prevents relapse but carries the highest Jarisch-Herxheimer risk; low-dose penicillin causes fewer reactions but more relapses. Patients must be closely monitored after the first dose for a potentially fatal Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, and critically ill patients should be resuscitated before specific treatment.

evidence.reference_title: Louse-borne relapsing fever (Borrelia recurrentis infection).
evidence.snippet: Complete cure with prevention of relapses is achievable with a single oral dose of 500 mg tetracycline or 500 mg erythromycin stearate.

evidence.reference_title: Tetracycline versus penicillin in the treatment of louse-borne relapsing fever.
evidence.snippet: Thus, tetracycline is recommended as first choice therapy and a single dose is sufficient for treatment of LBRF patients.

evidence.reference_title: Treatment of louse-borne relapsing fever with low dose penicillin or tetracycline: a clinical trial.
evidence.snippet: As mortality is linked to severe JHR, and most relapses are clinically mild and easily treated, these results speak in favour of using low-dose penicillin to initiate the treatment of relapsing fever.
